_note: The standard Italian pronunciation rules in the right-hand column of /pronuncia (AusspracheRegeln.astro), in teaching order. `match` is a regular expression tested on the lower-case word without an article: if it matches, the rule is listed under “For this word”. A rule without `match` is general and is never highlighted. `mark` (optional) is the stressed syllable, shown in bold. Standard Italian (italiano standard) is the model; what a learner will hear in daily life from other regions (gorgia toscana, the voiced or voiceless s, the Roman gli) is in `regional` notes only, never as a second mode. Rule ids are the old slot ids where the topic is the same (lang-kurz, ei-ie, betonung, auslaut, r, sch-st-sp = sc/sch, s, ig = c/g, h) and descriptive ids for the new ones (e-o, doppie, gl, gn, z, qu, raddoppiamento, elisione). The sounds are given in IPA between slashes; open/closed e and o are only marked in dictionaries, so they are taught for listening, not demanded in speech. Not yet reviewed by a teacher.

rules.title: The vowels: clear and pure
rules.text: Italian writes five vowels: a, e, i, o, u. Each one stays pure: no gliding (no is not “noh-oo”) and no weak “uh” in unstressed syllables. This includes the last vowel of a word, which English and French speakers tend to swallow: fame, notte and bene end in a clear “eh”.

examples.note: both e's are clear, the last one too
o with round lips, final e clear
every vowel keeps its full sound

rules.title: Open and closed e and o
rules.text: In a stressed syllable, e and o each have two possible sounds: closed /e/ /o/ and open /ɛ/ /ɔ/. In writing they look the same, except that a final stressed e takes è (open) or é (closed). A few words are told apart only by this: pèsca (peach, open) and pésca (fishing, closed); vènti (winds) and vénti (twenty). Dictionaries mark it; most Italians use the two sounds differently by region, so no one expects you to get it exactly right. Learn it by ear, especially the words that carry an accent: è (is) is open, perché is closed.

regional.note: In much of the north and in Sicily the open/closed contrast is weaker or follows local habit; Tuscan and Roman speech is closest to the dictionary.

rules.title: Two vowels together
rules.text: i or u next to another vowel is weak and normally forms one syllable with it (a dittongo): piano, quando, uomo, noi. Two strong vowels (a, e, o) next to each other are two syllables: teatro, paese. When the i or u itself is stressed, the vowels also split (an iato): zio is zì-o, farmacia is far-ma-cì-a, paura is pa-ù-ra.

examples.note: zì-o: the i is stressed, two syllables

rules.title: Word stress
rules.text: Every word has one strong syllable. Most Italian words are stressed on the second-to-last syllable (parole piane): casa, amico, parlare. Some are stressed on the last syllable (parole tronche) and always have a written accent there: città, caffè. Some are stressed on the third-to-last (parole sdrucciole): telefono, medico, macchina. The stress is almost never written, so learn it with the word.

rules.title: Written accents
rules.text: A word stressed on its last vowel always has a written accent: città, università, perché, caffè, più, può. Inside a word the accent is not written, except in a few dictionary cases. Short words use the accent to be told apart: è (is) and e (and); dà (gives) and da (from); là (there) and la (the); sì (yes) and si (oneself). Grave (à è ì ò ù) is the usual accent. The acute (é) is used on closed e: perché, né, sé, poiché.

rules.title: Double consonants
rules.text: A written double consonant is a long consonant: hold it about twice as long as a single one, and make the vowel before it short. It changes the word: pala (shovel), palla (ball); caro (dear), carro (cart); nono (ninth), nonno (grandfather); sete (thirst), sette (seven); casa (house), cassa (crate, till). English does this between words (“black cat”, “good dog”), but never inside one. After the stop (p, t, c, b, d, g) you hold the closure silently, then release it. gn, gl, sc and z between vowels are always long too: ogni, figlio, pesce, pizza.

rules.title: r and rr
rules.text: A single r is one quick tap of the tongue tip behind the top teeth: caro, sera, parlare. rr is a trill, several quick taps: carro, terra, correre. A word that starts with r also trills: rosso, Roma. The difference changes the word: caro (dear) and carro (cart); era (was) and erra (wanders). Some Italians say r in the throat (the erre moscia): you will hear it, but you don't need to copy it.

rules.title: c and g: soft and hard
rules.text: Before e or i, c is /tʃ/ (like ch in “church”) and g is /dʒ/ (like j in “jam”): cena, cinema, gelato, giorno. Before a, o, u, they are hard: /k/ and /g/: casa, cosa, gatto, gusto. To get the hard sound before e or i, Italian adds h: che, chi, ghetto, spaghetti. To get the soft sound before a, o, u, it adds a silent i: ciao, cioè, giorno, giusto. So ch is never “church” and gh is never silent.

examples.note: ci + a: the i is silent
gi + o: the i is silent

regional.note: In Tuscany a c between vowels often sounds like a breathy h (la casa → “la hasa”): the gorgia toscana. It is not the standard; don't copy it.

rules.title: sc and sch
rules.text: Before e or i, sc is /ʃ/, like sh in “ship”: scena, sci, pesce, scegliere. Before a, o, u, and before h, it is /sk/: scala, scuola, scheda, schiena. Between vowels /ʃ/ is long: pesce, lascia. A word can start with s + consonant (sp-, st-, sb-, sc-) without any extra vowel before it: scuola, studente, spesa. It is not “esk-”, “escuola”.

rules.title: gl: the “gli” sound
rules.text: gl before i is one sound, /ʎ/: the tongue presses its middle against the roof of the mouth, like “lli” in “million”, but longer and tighter. It is long between vowels: figlio, famiglia, aglio, meglio, and in the article gli. It is not “g” + “l” and not a plain l. A few learned words keep gl as /gl/: glicine, negligente. Before a, e, o, u, gl is also /gl/: gloria, inglese.

regional.note: In Rome and parts of the south, gli between vowels is often a long y sound (figlio ~ “fijjo”). It is local, not the standard.

rules.title: gn
rules.text: gn is one sound, /ɲ/: like ny in “canyon”, or the gn of French “agneau”. Press the middle of the tongue against the roof of the mouth. It is long between vowels: ogni, bagno, signora. It is not “g” + “n” (not “BAG-no”): gnocchi is “nyok-ki”.

rules.title: z
rules.text: z is a ts or a dz: both start with the tongue against the teeth and are released as a hiss. Examples: zio, pizza, grazie, stazione (all /ts/); zero, zona, mezzo (/dz/). Italians themselves vary, so for a learner it matters only that you say one of them: not an English buzzing z, not Spanish th (/θ/), and not just s. -zione is always /ts/; the double zz is long: pizza, ragazza. Only a few pairs depend on the difference.

regional.note: In the north pranzo, mezzo and zero have /dz/ (voiced); in the centre and south the same words often have /ts/. Both are normal.

rules.title: s
rules.text: s is /s/ (as in “sun”) at the start of a word before a vowel and before p, t, c, f, q: sole, sera, sport, stare. Before b, d, g, l, m, n, r, v it is voiced /z/, as in “zoo”: sbaglio, sdraiare, slitta, smettere, snello, sveglia. Between vowels, s is voiced in the north (casa, rosa, museo) and voiceless in the centre and south; both are fine. ss is always voiceless and long: cassa, rosso, basso.

regional.note: Between vowels: s is voiced /z/ in the north (casa, museo), voiceless /s/ in the south. In Tuscany it is mostly voiced; Rome is mixed. Both are heard.

rules.title: h is silent
rules.text: The letter h is never pronounced. It has only two jobs: it separates four forms of avere from words that sound the same (ho / o, hai / ai, ha / a, hanno / anno), and it makes c and g hard before e and i (che, chi, ghetto). In foreign words it is also silent: hotel, hobby.

examples.note: you have: sounds like ai (to the)

rules.title: qu
rules.text: qu is /kw/: the u is spoken. Say it like “qu” in “quick”: quando, questo, quattro, qui. This differs from Spanish, where the u of que and qui is silent. cu before a vowel is often the same: cuore, cuoco.

rules.title: Words that run together
rules.text: Italian is spoken with no stop between words. Listen for the raddoppiamento sintattico: after some short words and after any word stressed on its last vowel, the first consonant of the next word is long. a casa sounds like “ak-kasa”, è vero like “ev-vero”, più tardi like “piut-tardi”. It is not written and it is not needed to be understood, but you will hear it, mostly in central and southern speech.

regional.note: Raddoppiamento is typical of Tuscany, Rome and the south; speakers in the north often leave it out.

rules.title: Elision: the apostrophe
rules.text: An apostrophe shows that a vowel was dropped before another vowel. The two words are said as one: l'amico, un'amica, quest'anno, c'è, dov'è, nell'ufficio. Mind the difference in writing: un amico (masculine, no apostrophe) but un'amica (feminine, apostrophe), because the apostrophe stands for the missing a of una.
